problemText: In The Travels, Marco Polo describes the Chinese city of Kinsay (Hangzhou) around 1300, writing that on every market-day "all those squares are thronged and crammed with purchasers, and with the traders who have brought in stores of provisions by land or water". This description is best used as evidence that —
choices: Chinese commercial cities declined sharply once they came under Mongol rule after 1200
Kinsay was a hub of sustained large-scale commerce in the Silk Roads network
Overland caravan trade had entirely replaced maritime shipping into Chinese ports by 1300
Foreign merchants were formally barred from trading directly in major Yuan-era Chinese cities
hints: Ask what the sheer scale of buying and selling in Kinsay's markets, described on an ordinary market day, reveals about China's place in Afro-Eurasian trade networks around 1300.
Rule out any answer describing decline, isolation, or the disappearance of overland trade — the passage describes routine, thriving commerce.

problemText: Marco Polo, a Venetian merchant, writes that Kinsay's markets were so crowded that "no one would believe it possible that victuals enough could be provided for their consumption" unless they saw the scene themselves. This phrasing most directly reflects which point about Marco Polo's perspective as a source?
choices: He assumed European readers lacked a comparable frame of reference for such scale
He served as a Mongol tax official reporting Kinsay's market revenue to Kublai Khan
He had never personally traveled to Kinsay and relied entirely on secondhand rumors
He wrote the passage as a private diary entry never intended for any audience
hints: Notice Marco Polo frames the market's scale as something readers would need to see with their own eyes to believe.
Think about who Marco Polo was writing for — a European audience with no direct experience of a city like Kinsay.

problemText: Ibn Battuta describes the East African coastal town he calls "Kulwa" (Kilwa) around 1330: "Kulwa is a very fine and substantially built town, and all its buildings are of wood." This description is best used as evidence for which development in the Indian Ocean trade network, 1200-1450?
choices: The decline of East African coastal trade following Portuguese arrival in the region
The dominance of overland caravan routes over all Indian Ocean maritime commerce by 1300
The wealth port cities on the Indian Ocean network's African terminus had accumulated
The abandonment of Swahili coastal cities entirely in favor of inland farming settlements
hints: Kilwa sits at the East African end of the Indian Ocean network — think about what generated a 'fine and substantially built' town there.
Rule out answers describing decline or land-based (not maritime) trade dominance.

problemText: Ibn Battuta adds of Kulwa (Kilwa) that "Its inhabitants are constantly engaged in military expeditions, for their country is contiguous to the heathen Zanj." This detail is best explained by which historical situation facing Swahili coast city-states in this period?
choices: Kilwa's rulers had converted to Christianity and fought religious wars against Muslim neighbors
Mongol expansion had pushed nomadic raiders as far south as the East African coast
European colonial administrations of the sixteenth century required Swahili cities to maintain large standing armies
Wealthy cities like Kilwa bordered non-Muslim inland peoples and had to defend their wealth
hints: Ask what wealthy coastal trading cities would need to defend against non-Muslim inland neighbors.
'Zanj' refers to non-Muslim African peoples inland from the coast, not a European power.

problemText: Al-Umari reports that during Mansa Musa's 1324 stop in Cairo, the Cairenes "exchanged gold until they depressed its value in Egypt and caused its price to fall." This effect is best explained by which cause?
choices: Egyptian merchants had discovered a new gold mine near Cairo shortly before Mansa Musa's arrival
Mansa Musa distributed such an enormous quantity of gold that Cairo's supply suddenly increased
The Mamluk government deliberately devalued its currency to reduce Mali's political influence in Egypt
Trans-Saharan trade routes had closed, cutting off Cairo's usual gold supply from the south
hints: A sudden crash in gold's price means gold suddenly became much more abundant in Cairo — where did that gold come from?
Mansa Musa's hajj is famous for the sheer volume of gold he gave away along the way.

problemText: The Catalan Atlas (1375), made by the Majorcan cartographer Abraham Cresques for the king of Aragon, captions its image of Mansa Musa as "this king is the richest and most noble lord of all this region on account of the abundance of gold that is gathered in his land." This caption most directly reflects which point about the map as a historical source?
choices: It shows that Mali's gold wealth was already widely known across Europe by the late 1300s
It proves that Cresques personally traveled to Mali to verify Mansa Musa's wealth firsthand
It demonstrates that Aragon and Mali had signed a formal trade treaty guaranteeing gold shipments
It shows that most European mapmakers of this era considered West Africa unimportant to Mediterranean commerce
hints: The Catalan Atlas was made in Europe, for a European king, decades after Mansa Musa's famous 1324 hajj through Cairo.
Ask what the caption's emphasis on gold reveals about how Europeans had come to view West Africa.

problemText: Marco Polo describes the Great Khan's messengers finding "at every twenty-five miles of the journey a station which they call Yamb, or, as we should say, the Horse-Post-House." This relay system most directly contributed to which development across Mongol-controlled Eurasia, 1200-1450?
choices: The permanent unification of the four khanates under a single Mongol emperor after 1260
The replacement of overland Silk Roads trade with Indian Ocean maritime routes
Mass conversion of the Mongol elite to Christianity spread by traveling missionaries
The Pax Mongolica's relative safety and speed of long-distance communication across the empire
hints: A relay of fresh horses and lodging every 25 miles is built for speed and reliability of communication over enormous distances.
Connect the yam system to the broader Pax Mongolica idea covered in this unit.

problemText: Marco Polo adds that at yam stations, messengers "find all the rooms furnished with fine beds and all other necessary articles in rich silk". Read alongside accounts of the extreme violence Mongol armies used against resisting cities, this description of yam-station comfort best illustrates which point about the Mongol Empire?
choices: Mongol rulers spent lavishly on messengers while leaving the general population without resources
The yam system existed only in regions the Mongols had not yet fully conquered
The same empire capable of brutal conquest also invested heavily in effective, pragmatic administration
Mongol administrators imported all luxury goods from conquered Song China rather than producing them locally
hints: Contrast the violence of Mongol conquest with the investment shown in comfortable, well-supplied relay stations.
The question is about what kind of empire the Mongols built after conquest, not about the conquest itself.

problemText: Marco Polo reports that Yuan paper money was "issued with as much solemnity and authority as if they were of pure gold or silver", with officials' seals stamped on every sheet. Carried back to Europe, this account of Chinese paper currency best illustrates which broader pattern in the period 1200-1450?
choices: Trade networks carried not just goods but also knowledge of commercial technologies across regions
European merchants had already adopted paper currency well before contact with Yuan China
The Mongols quickly suppressed all pre-existing Chinese financial practices they encountered after conquest
Silver and gold coinage had been fully abandoned across Afro-Eurasia by the late 1200s
hints: Paper money is a commercial technology, not a good like silk or gold — think about what else besides goods moved along trade networks.
Marco Polo is reporting something novel to him back to a European audience.

problemText: Boccaccio writes that the plague reaching Florence in 1348 "had had its origin some years before in the East" before, as he writes, it "had spread into the West." This account is best explained by which cause?
choices: Deliberate biological warfare waged by Mongol armies against Italian city-states
A sudden collapse of Silk Roads trade that stranded infected merchants in Italian ports
The same well-traveled trade routes that carried goods across Afro-Eurasia also carried disease
An independent outbreak of disease that arose separately and simultaneously within Florence itself
hints: The unit's key point is that the same routes carrying goods across Afro-Eurasia could carry disease too — think about what physically enabled the plague's westward spread.
Rule out any answer involving deliberate human action (warfare) or a coincidental, unconnected outbreak.

problemText: Neo-Confucian thought diffused from Song China to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan in this period. Which statement best describes how Japan's adoption of Neo-Confucianism differed from Korea's and Vietnam's?
choices: Japan adopted both Neo-Confucian philosophy and the civil-service examination system in full, exactly as Korea and Vietnam did
Japan adopted Neo-Confucian philosophy without adopting the examination-based bureaucracy, remaining governed by hereditary samurai rule
Japan rejected Neo-Confucian philosophy outright while adopting only the examination system
Korea and Vietnam rejected Neo-Confucian philosophy outright while only Japan adopted it
hints: Korea and Vietnam adopted the exam-based bureaucracy along with Neo-Confucian thought; Japan's case is the exception.
Rule out any answer claiming full adoption of the exam system in Japan, or rejection of the philosophy anywhere.

problemText: The Black Death, having spread westward along Mongol-secured trade routes, killed an estimated one-third or more of Europe's population by the mid-1300s. Which of the following best describes a documented downstream social and economic consequence of this population loss in Europe?
choices: Labor became more abundant, driving wages down and strengthening lords' control over serfs
European feudal obligations were immediately abolished by royal decree in response to the plague
The plague had no lasting economic effect at all once population levels began recovering within a few years
Severe labor shortages increased surviving peasants' bargaining power, contributing to the erosion of some feudal labor obligations
hints: A smaller labor force generally increases, not decreases, surviving workers' bargaining leverage.
Rule out any answer describing an immediate legal abolition of feudalism or a quick, effect-free recovery — neither matches the actual, gradual social change.

problemText: Indian Ocean sailors used two ship designs to work the monsoon cycle: the dhow, common in the western Indian Ocean, and the Chinese junk, common on the network's eastern end. What technological feature let the dhow sail effectively across and against the wind, rather than only downwind?
choices: its triangular lateen sail
its use of a magnetic compass for navigation
its reliance on oar-powered propulsion rather than sails
its flat-bottomed hull design borrowed from Chinese junks
hints: The lateen sail's triangular shape is what let sailors tack across and against the wind.
Rule out the compass (a navigation aid, not a sailing-angle technology) and oar power — the dhow was a sailing vessel.

problemText: Arab, Persian, Gujarati, and Chinese merchants settled semi-permanently in foreign Indian Ocean ports, often intermarrying locally and maintaining shared religious or commercial ties across vast distances. This pattern of diasporic merchant settlement is best understood as addressing which underlying challenge of long-distance trade?
choices: the absence of any common written language among Indian Ocean merchants
the difficulty of establishing trust and enforcing business agreements between merchants from distant, unfamiliar societies
the lack of monsoon wind knowledge among foreign merchants arriving in new ports
a shortage of skilled shipbuilders in Indian Ocean port cities
hints: Ask what settling permanently, intermarrying, and sharing religion or commercial ties across distant ports would actually solve for merchants doing business with strangers.
Rule out answers about language, wind knowledge, or shipbuilding — none of those is the underlying problem diasporic communities addressed.

problemText: After the mid-1200s, the Mongol Empire fractured into four major successor states, still linked by shared Mongol lineage but increasingly independent in practice. Which of the following is one of these four khanates?
choices: the Ottoman Empire in Anatolia
the rival Mamluk Sultanate ruling Egypt and Syria
the Yuan Dynasty in China
the Byzantine Empire in Constantinople
hints: The four khanates were the Yuan Dynasty, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate, and the Golden Horde.
Rule out the Ottomans, Mamluks, and Byzantines — none were Mongol successor states.

problemText: Mongol conquest was frequently brutal — cities that resisted were sometimes destroyed as a deterrent. Yet once territory was secured, Mongol rulers generally practiced religious tolerance and employed skilled foreign administrators regardless of ethnicity or faith. Which conclusion about the Mongol Empire's overall legacy do these two facts together best support?
choices: the Mongols were destructive conquerors whose empire left behind no lasting positive institutional legacy of any real kind
Mongol tolerance of foreign administrators proves that Mongol conquest itself was largely peaceful and bloodless
Mongol rulers only tolerated religions and administrators that were ethnically Mongol
Mongol conquest and Mongol administration should be evaluated as two distinct phases with different, even contradictory, characteristics
hints: The key point is a genuine tension: brutal conquest followed by pragmatic, tolerant administration — hold both facts as true rather than picking one to explain away the other.
Rule out any answer denying the conquest's real violence or denying the administration's real tolerance.

problemText: Caravanserai were roadside inns spaced roughly a day's journey apart along Silk Roads routes. What was their primary function for merchant caravans?
choices: providing rest, resupply, and safe overnight storage of goods
collecting customs duties on behalf of the Mongol government
training merchants in the use of bills of exchange
housing only the imperial yam relay messengers, with merchants turned away at the door
hints: Think about what a caravan crossing hundreds of miles of overland route would need at regular intervals.
Rule out the yam messenger system (a related but distinct Mongol institution) and customs collection or merchant training — neither is the caravanserai's stated function.

problemText: Overland trade connecting China, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean existed for more than a thousand years before the Mongol conquests of the 1200s, rising and falling with political stability along the route. Given this, which claim about the Mongols' role in Silk Roads history is most defensible?
choices: the Mongols invented overland Eurasian trade, since no contact between China and the Mediterranean existed earlier
the Mongols secured and intensified an already-ancient network by unifying much of the route under one political authority
the Mongols had no meaningful effect on Silk Roads trade volume in either direction
the Mongols redirected all Silk Roads trade toward maritime routes instead of overland ones
hints: The key distinction is inventing a network versus securing and intensifying one that already existed for centuries.
Rule out any answer denying the Mongols had any effect, or claiming they shifted trade toward the sea — that describes a much later period.

problemText: In the trans-Saharan trade network, salt mined in the Sahara moved south into West Africa, while gold mined in West African goldfields moved north across the desert. This exchange is best explained by which economic logic?
choices: West Africa produced both gold and salt in equal abundance, making the exchange largely ceremonial rather than economic
salt was more valuable than gold everywhere in the medieval world
each region traded away a resource it had in abundance for one it lacked
North Africa mined its own gold and had no need to trade for West African gold
hints: Salt was scarce in tropical West Africa but abundant in the Sahara; gold was the reverse.
Rule out any answer denying real scarcity on one side or the other, or claiming a universal value ranking between salt and gold.

problemText: Much of the gold that reached Mali's trade routes was mined outside Mali's own core territory, in goldfields such as the Akan forest region and the Bambuk/Bure area, controlled by other peoples and polities. Given this, which statement best explains the actual source of Mali's imperial wealth?
choices: Mali directly owned and mined nearly all of West Africa's gold within its own core territory
Mali's wealth came mainly from tribute paid by the neighboring Songhai Empire
Mali's rulers earned their wealth primarily through direct diplomatic gifts from Mamluk Egypt
Mali grew wealthy chiefly by controlling and taxing the trade routes and market cities through which gold from various sources moved north
hints: Distinguish between owning a gold source outright and controlling/taxing the routes gold traveled along.
Rule out any answer requiring Mali to directly mine most of the gold itself, or crediting Songhai tribute or Mamluk gifts — neither matches the historical record.

problemText: Mansa Musa and other Mali rulers converted to Islam, partly because shared religion with North African trading partners eased business and diplomatic ties. Which statement most accurately describes the broader pattern of religious change across the Mali Empire that resulted from this trade-driven conversion?
choices: conversion to Islam was concentrated among rulers and urban merchant classes, while traditional African religions persisted widely, especially in rural areas
the entire population of the Mali Empire converted to Islam within a single generation of Mansa Musa's reign
Mansa Musa's conversion had no influence on religious practice anywhere else in the empire
traditional African religions were formally banned throughout Mali immediately after Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj
hints: Conversion concentrated among rulers and urban merchants while traditional religions persisted widely in rural areas.
Rule out any answer claiming universal, immediate conversion or a formal ban on other religions — neither is supported.

problemText: Of the three major Afro-Eurasian trade networks active in the period 1200-1450 — the Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean network, and the trans-Saharan network — which one relied primarily on seasonal monsoon winds rather than overland caravan routes or camel crossings?
choices: the Silk Roads
the Indian Ocean network
the trans-Saharan network
all three relied equally on monsoon winds
hints: Only one of the three networks was maritime, powered by seasonally reversing winds.
The Silk Roads were overland caravan routes; trans-Saharan trade used camel caravans across desert, not ships.

problemText: The Strait of Malacca, the narrow sea passage connecting the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea, was controlled at different points by Srivijaya, then Majapahit, then the Sultanate of Malacca. Controlling this chokepoint was valuable chiefly because it allowed a ruling power to —
choices: block Chinese junks and Arab dhows alike from ever reaching any Indian Ocean trading ports west of Malacca
monopolize the mining and sale of gold across the entire Southeast Asian mainland and archipelago
tax the huge volume of maritime trade passing between East Asia, India, Africa, and the Middle East
control the overland Silk Roads caravan routes running through Central Asia toward the Mediterranean
hints: Nearly all maritime trade between East Asia and India/Africa/the Middle East had to pass through this narrow strait.
Rule out any answer about gold mining or overland Central Asian routes — Malacca's value was maritime chokepoint taxation.

problemText: Long-distance merchants in this period relied on financial innovations such as bills of exchange (Italian and Islamic banking), hundi (an Indian credit network), and Yuan-issued paper money to reduce the risks of long-distance trade. What problem did these innovations chiefly solve?
choices: the absence of any common language for negotiating prices between merchants of different regions
the unpredictability of monsoon wind patterns in the Indian Ocean
the lack of camels suitable for carrying trade goods across the Sahara
the danger and inefficiency of physically transporting large quantities of coin across long, often unsafe distances
hints: Each of these credit instruments let a merchant avoid physically carrying valuable metal across dangerous distances.
Rule out answers about language, monsoon winds, or camels — none of those is what credit instruments address.

problemText: Marco Polo's end-to-end journey from Europe to China and back is often cited in popular accounts of the Silk Roads. Historians note that this kind of complete journey was exceptional rather than typical. Which statement best explains why?
choices: the Silk Roads worked as a network of regional segments, with most merchants trading only part of the route at hub cities
almost no merchant besides Marco Polo ever completed the full overland journey from Venice to Yuan China
the Mongol Yuan government formally banned merchants from traveling the entire route in a single continuous journey
goods reached Europe from China only by the long Indian Ocean sea route, since overland caravan routes had already closed a century earlier
hints: Most goods changed hands repeatedly at hub cities like Samarkand or Bukhara rather than traveling with a single merchant the whole way.
Rule out any answer claiming near-total absence of travel, a Mongol travel ban, or an exclusively maritime route — none matches the historical record.
